q: Under Ind AS 115, a promised good or service is distinct only if:
o: It is sold separately by the entity at some point during the period
The customer can benefit from it alone and it is separately identifiable
It has a stand-alone selling price that is directly observable in the market
The entity can identify a separate cost centre for that promise
why: Both the capable of being distinct test and the distinct within the context of the contract test must be met. Observable stand-alone selling price is relevant to allocation, not to whether the promise is distinct.

q: An entity sells equipment and provides complex installation that significantly customises the equipment. Under Ind AS 115 the likely conclusion is:
o: One obligation, as the goods and installation form a combined output
Two obligations, since the installation could be performed by others
Two obligations, since the equipment has an observable separate price
Revenue is deferred in full until the warranty period has expired
why: Significant customisation means the entity is providing a combined output, so the promises are not separately identifiable within the contract. That a third party could theoretically install does not override the integration test.

q: The constraint on variable consideration requires an entity to include variable amounts only to the extent that:
o: The amount is more likely than not to be received from the customer
The variable element is less than 10 percent of the transaction price
The customer has confirmed the variable amount to the entity in writing
It is highly probable no significant reversal of revenue will occur
why: Ind AS 115 uses the highly probable no significant reversal threshold, which is a higher hurdle than more likely than not. There is no percentage safe harbour for variable consideration.

q: Which factor MOST indicates the entity is a principal rather than an agent?
o: The entity has full discretion in establishing the price for the good
The entity earns a commission set as a fixed percentage of each sale
The entity controls the specified good before it passes to the buyer
The name of the entity appears on the invoice sent to the customer
why: Control of the specified good before transfer is the overarching principle, with price discretion and inventory risk serving only as indicators supporting it. Invoice branding and commission form are presentation features that do not determine the conclusion.

q: A performance obligation is satisfied over time if the entity performance creates an asset with no alternative use AND:
o: The customer settles the agreed contract price in equal instalments
The entity has an enforceable right to payment for work completed
The term of the contract extends beyond a period of twelve months
The entity uses percentage of completion in its internal costing
why: The no alternative use criterion must be paired with an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date, including a reasonable profit margin. Instalment payments and contract length are not criteria in the standard.

q: An entity recognises revenue but its right to consideration is conditional on completing a further milestone. The amount should be presented as:
o: A contract asset, as the right is conditioned on more than time
A trade receivable, since the related revenue has been recognised
Deferred revenue within current liabilities on the balance sheet
Other current assets, with no further disclosure being required
why: A receivable arises only when the right to consideration is unconditional, needing nothing beyond passage of time. Where a further performance condition exists, the balance is a contract asset and carries different disclosure and impairment considerations.

q: A contract includes a significant financing component when:
o: Any payment by the customer is deferred beyond a period of thirty days
The contract price exceeds the cash selling price by any amount at all
The customer settles the contract price in a foreign currency instead
Payment timing gives either party a significant benefit of financing
why: The test is whether the payment timing provides a significant financing benefit to either party, assessed against the cash selling price. A practical expedient allows the component to be ignored where the period between transfer and payment is one year or less.

q: An entity grants a customer a right to return goods within 30 days. Under Ind AS 115 the entity should:
o: Recognise full revenue and disclose the return right as contingent
Defer all of the revenue until the thirty day return period lapses
Recognise revenue net of expected returns, with a refund liability
Treat the right of return as a separate performance obligation
why: Return rights are variable consideration, so revenue excludes expected returns and a refund liability plus an asset for the right to recover goods are recognised. A right of return is expressly not a separate performance obligation under the standard.

q: Consideration payable to a customer that is not in exchange for a distinct good or service should be:
o: Accounted for as a reduction of the transaction price recognised
Recognised as a selling and distribution expense as it is incurred
Capitalised as a contract cost and amortised over the contract term
Recognised as a separate performance obligation in the contract
why: Payments to a customer reduce the transaction price unless they buy a distinct good or service at fair value. Classifying such payments as marketing expense inflates both revenue and expenses.

q: Which allocation basis does Ind AS 115 require for the transaction price across multiple performance obligations?
o: The relative cost incurred on each of the separate performance obligations
Relative stand-alone selling prices, estimated where not observable
Equal allocation of the transaction price across the obligations
The individual amounts stated in the contract in every situation
why: Allocation follows relative stand-alone selling prices, estimated using approaches such as adjusted market assessment, expected cost plus margin, or residual where permitted. Contractual stated prices are used only where they represent stand-alone selling prices.

q: An audit team is testing revenue cut-off for goods shipped FOB destination. The MOST relevant evidence around the year end is:
o: Sales invoices dated during the final week of the financial year
The reconciliation of the sales ledger control account at the year end
Purchase orders received from customers before the year end date
Proof of delivery evidencing the date the customer obtained control
why: With FOB destination terms, control transfers on delivery, so delivery evidence determines the correct period. Invoice dates are set by the entity and can be manipulated, which is why they are the weaker choice.

q: Incremental costs of obtaining a contract, such as a sales commission payable only on winning the contract, should be:
o: Expensed as incurred in every case, whatever the length of contract
Netted against the revenue recognised on the related contract
Recognised as an asset if recoverable, with a one year expedient
Recognised as a contract liability until the contract completes
why: Ind AS 115 requires capitalisation of recoverable incremental acquisition costs, with an expedient permitting immediate expense where the amortisation period would not exceed one year. Salaries payable regardless of contract success are not incremental and are expensed.

q: An entity sells a machine with a two year assurance type warranty required by law and an optional extended warranty. The correct treatment is:
o: Both of the warranties are separate performance obligations of the entity
The assurance warranty is a provision, the extended one an obligation
Both of the warranties are provisions recognised under Ind AS 37
Neither warranty is recognised until a valid claim actually arises
why: Assurance warranties that merely confirm the product meets agreed specifications are provisions, while service type warranties sold separately are performance obligations with allocated revenue. Treating the assurance warranty as a performance obligation would improperly defer revenue.

q: For a bill and hold arrangement, revenue can be recognised only if, in addition to the customer having requested the arrangement, the:
o: Goods are identified as the customer property and ready for transfer
Invoice has been raised and payment received fully in advance
Goods held are insured by the entity against loss or damage in store
Customer has provided a written and signed purchase order form
why: Ind AS 115 sets specific criteria including a substantive reason for the arrangement, identification of the goods as the customer property, readiness for transfer, and inability of the entity to redirect them. Invoicing and payment alone do not establish transfer of control.

q: Which measure of progress would ordinarily be INAPPROPRIATE for a service contract where the entity efforts are expended evenly?
o: Time elapsed as a proportion of the total contract period agreed
Costs incurred relative to the total costs expected on the contract
Surveys of the performance that has been completed to that date
Units of standard product delivered where delivery is uneven
why: A units delivered measure would distort revenue where deliveries do not track the pattern of effort under an evenly expended service contract. Time elapsed, cost to cost, and surveys of work performed all track the transfer of the service more faithfully.

q: Under the expected value method for estimating variable consideration, the entity should:
o: Use the single most likely outcome of the possible amounts
Use the maximum possible amount of consideration that is receivable
Use the probability weighted sum, suiting many similar contracts
Use the amount stated in the contract whatever the probability
why: The expected value method is the probability weighted approach and fits populations of many similar contracts, such as volume rebates. The most likely amount method is the alternative and suits contracts with only two possible outcomes.

q: An auditor identifies that side letters granting extended return rights were not provided to the finance team. The primary revenue audit risk is:
o: Overstatement of revenue, as the true terms alter transfer of control
Understatement of the trade payables balance at the reporting date
Misclassification between current and non-current assets on the balance sheet
Understatement of the deferred tax asset recognised in the accounts
why: Undisclosed side letters change the substance of the arrangement and typically mean revenue was recognised too early or at too high an amount. This is a recognised fraud risk area, which is why searching for side agreements is a standard revenue procedure.

Consideration is received, or unconditionally due, before transfer
The customer has disputed an invoice raised on it by the entity
The entity has performed the work but has not yet raised an invoice
why: A contract liability reflects the obligation to transfer goods or services for consideration already received or unconditionally due. Performance ahead of invoicing produces a contract asset, which is the opposite position.
